1	# Phase 3 plan: continuous performance work
     2	
     3	Starts when the TypeScript release from [03-plan-typescript-release.md](03-plan-typescript-release.md) works end to end. That release is the baseline: every later change is compared with it, in a real browser, on workloads a reader would notice.
     4	
     5	Budget IDs (P1–P7) are defined in [02-product-spec.md](02-product-spec.md). Phase 1 numbers are in [01-landscape.md](01-landscape.md), section 5.3.
     6	
     7	## 1. What Phase 1 already established
     8	
     9	| Fact | Consequence for this plan |
    10	|---|---|
    11	| uPlot, plain JavaScript on Canvas 2D, drew 1,000,000 points in about 60 ms and appended a point in under 0.1 ms. | The TypeScript ceiling is high. Any other technology has to beat tuned TypeScript, not a naive version. |
    12	| Chart.js went from 13.7 s to 111 ms at 1,000,000 points by changing four options. | The largest wins are algorithmic (decimate, skip parsing, skip animation), not low-level. Look there first. |
    13	| Libraries creating one DOM node per point took 4–7 s at 100,000 points. | Node count is the first thing to watch in any regression. |
    14	| The Phase 1 timing method could not resolve below about 35 ms and missed off-thread rasterization. | The method is replaced before budgets become gates (section 3). |
    15	| Headless Chrome ran WebGL on a software rasterizer. | GPU paths are measured only in headed browsers on real hardware. |
    16	
    17	## 2. Workloads
    18	
    19	Each workload is a page in `bench/` that takes a library adapter, so the same page runs Axylo and the comparison libraries. Sizes cover what dashboards do and one step beyond.
    20	
    21	| ID | Workload | Sizes | What a reader would notice | Budget |
    22	|---|---|---|---|---|
    23	| W-first | Create one line chart and show it | 3×120; 1×10k; 1×100k; 1×1M; 10×100k | Delay before the chart appears | P1, P2 |
    24	| W-page | Create 24 small charts on one page | 24 × (3×120) | Dashboard load | P5 |
    25	| W-stream | Append one point per frame to a sliding window | 600; 10k; 100k window | Stutter | P3 |
    26	| W-replace | Replace all data | 10k; 100k | Delay after changing a filter | – |
    27	| W-hover | Sweep the pointer across the plot, 200 moves | 10k; 100k; 1M | Tooltip lag | P4 |
    28	| W-zoom | Wheel-zoom in and out 60 steps, then pan | 100k; 1M | Jerky zoom | – |
    29	| W-resize | Animate container width 1,200 → 400 → 1,200 px over 2 s | 24 charts; 1×100k | Jank while a sidebar opens | – |
    30	| W-bars | Stacked bars | 12×50; 5×2,000 | Delay before the chart appears | – |
    31	| W-scatter | Scatter with nearest-point hover | 10k; 100k; 1M | Tooltip lag, draw time | – |
    32	| W-load | Cold page load with the script-tag build and one chart | – | Time until the first chart is visible | P6 |
    33	| W-mem | Heap after create; after 1,000 create–destroy cycles; retained per 1M points | – | Tab memory, slow leak | P7 |
    34	
    35	Workloads without a budget get one when their first baseline exists. A workload is added when a user report or a profile shows a pattern these do not cover, and each addition records why.
    36	
    37	## 3. How to measure
    38	
    39	### 3.1 Metrics
    40	
    41	| Metric | How | Why this and not something simpler |
    42	|---|---|---|
    43	| Time to visible | `performance.mark` at call; completion taken from the first `requestAnimationFrame` callback **after** a frame in which the canvas content hash stopped changing, cross-checked on a sample of runs against a screenshot | The Phase 1 "second frame" method counted a frame as done when a library had only started. |
    44	| Main-thread blocking | Long Animation Frames API (`long-animation-frame` entries): total blocking duration and longest frame | Captures style, layout and paint work that script timers miss. |
    45	| Scripting cost of an operation | `performance.now()` around the call, plus a forced synchronous flush where the library defers | For microsecond-scale updates (append, hover) where frames are too coarse. |
    46	| Frame pacing | Intervals between `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks: p50, p95, p99, count over 1.5× the refresh interval | What stutter looks like. |
    47	| Interaction latency | Event Timing API (`event` entries: input delay, processing, presentation) for real dispatched pointer and key events | The same quantity INP reports. |
    48	| GPU and raster time | Chrome tracing (`devtools.timeline`, `gpu`) on selected runs | Canvas commands are cheap to issue and can be expensive to rasterize. |
    49	| Memory | `performance.measureUserAgentSpecificMemory()` where available; otherwise CDP `HeapProfiler.collectGarbage` then `Runtime.getHeapUsage` | Forced collection before reading, or the number is noise. |
    50	| Bytes | Minified, gzip and brotli size of each entry point; parse and compile time from a trace | Download and startup are part of every workload. |
    51	
    52	### 3.2 Environment
    53	
    54	| Dimension | Values |
    55	|---|---|
    56	| Browsers | Chrome stable, Firefox stable, Safari (WebKit on macOS), headed, with a real GPU. Edge on Windows for release runs. |
    57	| Hardware profiles | "Desktop": the reference machine. "Mid laptop": the same with 4× CPU throttling through CDP (Chromium only). "Phone": one real mid-range Android phone over USB, release runs only. |
    58	| Display | Fixed 1,440×900 window, device pixel ratio 1 and 2. |
    59	| Build | Production build of every library, pinned versions recorded in the result file. |
    60	| Isolation | Fresh browser context per run; no extensions; machine otherwise idle; power plan and browser version recorded. |
    61	
    62	The reference machine restarts often and has no permanent scratch space, so every run writes its results and environment record to `bench/history/` in the repository before it reports, and a run interrupted by a restart is discarded, never merged with a later one.
    63	
    64	### 3.3 Statistics
    65	
    66	- **Repetitions:** at least 20 fresh-context runs per workload and configuration; 50 for anything under 20 ms.
    67	- **Interleaving:** baseline and candidate alternate (A B A B …) within one session, so drift in machine state affects both.
    68	- **Summary:** median, with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval for the difference of medians. Tail metrics (p95, p99) for frame pacing and latency.
    69	- **Noise floor:** each session starts with an A-versus-A comparison of the baseline against itself. The observed difference is the noise floor for that session and is stored with the results.
    70	- **No transfer:** a result holds for the commit, browser version and machine it was measured on. Numbers are not carried from one commit to another or from Linux to Windows.
    71	
    72	### 3.4 Comparison libraries
    73	
    74	| Library | Configurations | Role |
    75	|---|---|---|
    76	| uPlot | Default | Speed reference. Budgets P2 and P3 are ratios to it. |
    77	| Chart.js | Default; documented fast path | The most deployed; shows default versus tuned. |
    78	| ECharts | Default; sampling on | Canvas with built-in large-data modes. |
    79	| Highcharts | Default; Boost | SVG with a WebGL escape hatch; non-commercial evaluation use only. |
    80	| Recharts | Default; dots and animation off | What most React users have today. |
    81	
    82	Adapters live in `bench/libs/`, start from the Phase 1 harness modules, and state in a comment every non-default option and the documentation page that recommends it. Versions are pinned and bumped once a quarter in a commit of their own, so a change in a competitor's number is never mistaken for a change in Axylo. Comparison numbers are published with the method, the versions and the configuration files.
    83	
    84	## 4. The improvement loop
    85	
    86	One iteration, written up as a short record in `bench/experiments/NNNN-title.md`:
    87	
    88	1. **Pick the target.** The workload furthest over its budget; if all budgets pass, the workload with the largest absolute time a reader waits. Not the most interesting code.
    89	2. **Find the bottleneck.** Record a Chrome performance profile of that workload at the production build with source maps. Attribute time to pipeline stages (normalize, scales, layout, scene, canvas commands, DOM text, raster) using `performance.measure` spans that exist in the build behind a flag. A stage is "the bottleneck" when it holds the largest share of blocking time, and worth attacking alone when that share is over 30%.
    90	3. **State a hypothesis** that can fail: "Layout takes 41% of W-page because every tick label is measured twice; caching measurements by font and string will cut W-page by at least 25%."
    91	4. **Build the smallest experiment** behind a flag or on a branch. No refactoring mixed in.
    92	5. **Measure** candidate against baseline with section 3's method on the target workload and on every other tracked workload.
    93	6. **Decide** with the rule in section 5 and write down the result, including when the hypothesis was wrong. Negative results stay in the repository so the same idea is not retried without new evidence.
    94	7. **Review.** Someone other than the author of the change checks the measurement and the record before it is merged.
    95	
    96	Expected order of attack, from Phase 1 evidence. Each is a hypothesis to test, not a commitment:
    97	
    98	| Order | Area | Why it is likely to matter |
    99	|---|---|---|
   100	| 1 | Work avoided: memoized stages, no relayout on data-only updates, decimation bounded by pixel width | The two-orders-of-magnitude gaps in Phase 1 all came from this class. |
   101	| 2 | Allocation in hot paths: typed columns end to end, reused path buffers, no per-point objects | Streaming and hover run every frame; garbage shows up as frame-pacing tails. |
   102	| 3 | Canvas command volume: one path per series, batched state changes, integer-aligned strokes | uPlot's approach; cheap to try. |
   103	| 4 | Text: measurement cache, fewer DOM writes, reuse of label elements | 24 charts multiply every text cost. |
   104	| 5 | Hit testing: binary search on sorted x, grid index for scatter | Bounds hover cost independent of point count. |
   105	| 6 | Partial redraw: separate canvas layer for cursor and focus; blit for streaming scroll | Removes full redraws from hover and append. |
   106	| 7 | Startup: module structure, lazy code for zoom and table view | Affects W-load on every page. |
   107	| 8 | Off-main-thread: `OffscreenCanvas` in a worker for very large series | High integration cost; only if 1–7 leave a budget failing. |
   108	| 9 | WebGL or WebGPU marks | Only if raster time, not script time, is the measured bottleneck at sizes users reach. |
   109	
   110	## 5. What makes a gain worth shipping
   111	
   112	All of the following must hold.
   113	
   114	| Condition | Threshold |
   115	|---|---|
   116	| The gain is real | The 95% confidence interval for the improvement in the target metric excludes zero, and the median improvement is at least twice that session's noise floor. |
   117	| The gain is large enough to matter | At least 5% on the target workload's primary metric, or it moves a workload from failing to passing its budget, or it removes at least one frame over budget per 300 in a pacing workload. |
   118	| Nothing else pays for it | No other tracked workload regresses by more than its noise floor or 2%, whichever is larger. This is checked in all three browsers. |
   119	| Bytes are accounted for | At most 0.3 kB gzipped per 5% gained on the target workload, and the DX7 size budget still holds. Larger costs need a workload moving from fail to pass. |
   120	| Correctness is unchanged | Scene snapshots are identical, or every difference is reviewed and approved. All fidelity property tests pass, in particular F2 (gaps) and F5 (extremes survive decimation). |
   121	| Complexity is paid for | A change that adds a new code path, a mode or a public option needs at least 20% on its target, or a budget moving from fail to pass. Otherwise the simpler code stays. |
   122	
   123	A gain a reader cannot perceive (for example 9 ms to 7 ms on a one-off render) ships only if it is free in bytes and complexity. Crossing a threshold a reader can perceive ranks above any percentage: one frame (16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz) for interaction and animation, 100 ms for a response to input, 1 s for a chart to appear.
   124	
   125	## 6. Catching regressions
   126	
   127	| When | What runs | Compared with | Action |
   128	|---|---|---|---|
   129	| Every pull request | Smoke set: W-first at 3×120 and 1×100k, W-stream at 600, W-hover at 100k, bytes. Chromium, 10 interleaved runs, about 3 minutes. | The merge base, built and run in the same job | Fail on a regression over 10% with a confidence interval excluding zero, or any size-budget breach. Otherwise post the table. |
   130	| Nightly | Full workload set, three browsers, desktop and throttled profiles, 20 runs | The previous night and the last release | Open an issue for any workload outside its noise band two nights running, with the commit range. |
   131	| Before a release | Full set plus the phone profile, Edge on Windows, and the comparison libraries | Budgets P1–P7 and the previous release | A failed budget blocks the release, or the budget is changed in the spec with a written reason. Never silently. |
   132	| Quarterly | Comparison library versions bumped; budgets expressed as ratios re-derived | – | Publish the updated comparison. |
   133	
   134	Pull-request runs use shared CI machines, so they compare two builds inside one job and never against stored numbers. Nightly and release runs use the reference machine and are the only source of absolute numbers.
   135	
   136	Results are appended to `bench/history/` as one JSON file per run with commit, browser versions, machine profile, noise floor and raw samples. A page in the documentation site charts that history with Axylo itself.
   137	
   138	Performance tests are held to the same honesty rules as functional tests: a budget is not relaxed to make a run pass, a known-slow workload is reported as failing until it is fixed, and a comparison that Axylo loses is published as measured.
   139	
   140	## 7. Where Rust could be justified, and what it would take
   141	
   142	### 7.1 Candidates
   143	
   144	A Rust experiment is worth running only for a stage that is a measured bottleneck on a tracked workload and is compute-bound on numeric data. Stages that mostly call browser APIs cannot gain: each call crosses the JavaScript–WebAssembly boundary and the browser does the work either way.
   145	
   146	| Stage | Could Rust help? | Reasoning |
   147	|---|---|---|
   148	| Decimation and aggregation over typed columns (min–max per pixel, binning, stacking) at 1M+ points | Possibly | Tight numeric loops over contiguous memory; SIMD is available in WebAssembly. JavaScript engines already compile such loops well, so the expected gain is small multiples at best. |
   149	| Spatial index build and query for scatter at 1M+ points | Possibly | Memory layout control matters; no browser API involved. |
   150	| Parsing large text inputs (CSV, ISO dates) into columns | Unlikely | Strings must be copied into WebAssembly memory and decoded; the copy often costs as much as the parse. |
   151	| Layout, tick generation, label fitting | No | Small inputs; dominated by text measurement, which is a browser call. |
   152	| Canvas 2D drawing | No | One boundary crossing per command. |
   153	| Rendering to a pixel buffer or to WebGL/WebGPU from Rust | Only as a separate product decision | It replaces the renderer rather than accelerating a stage, brings its own text rendering, and does nothing for the DOM-based accessibility layer. It would need a failing raster-bound budget that item 9 in section 4 could not fix in TypeScript. |
   154	
   155	### 7.2 Preconditions for starting an experiment
   156	
   157	1. A profile shows the stage holds at least 30% of blocking time on a tracked workload at a size users reach, and that workload fails its budget or is the largest remaining wait.
   158	2. The TypeScript version of that stage has already been tuned (typed arrays, no allocation in the loop, monomorphic call sites, pixel-bounded work) and independently reviewed as tuned. "Tuned" is a recorded claim with a profile attached, not an impression.
   159	3. The experiment has a written hypothesis with a number and a time ceiling.
   160	
   161	### 7.3 Evidence required to adopt
   162	
   163	The comparison is always end to end, on the workload, against the tuned TypeScript build, with section 3's method.
   164	
   165	| Question | Evidence required |
   166	|---|---|
   167	| Is the workload faster for the reader? | Median improvement of at least 20% on the workload's primary metric (not on the isolated function), confidence interval excluding zero, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari. A function-level microbenchmark is not evidence. |
   168	| What does startup cost? | Fetch, compile and instantiate time of the `.wasm`, cold and warm cache, on desktop and throttled profiles, included in W-load and in the first render of the affected workload. Stated as the number of operations needed to earn the startup cost back. |
   169	| What does data transfer cost? | Time to move columns into WebAssembly memory and results back, measured separately and included in the end-to-end number. If the design keeps columns in WebAssembly memory to avoid copies, the cost that imposes on `update`, `append` and memory (P7) is measured too. |
   170	| Where is the crossover? | The data size above which the Rust path wins end to end, including the costs above. It must be at or below sizes real users reach; a win only at 50M points is not a reason. |
   171	| Do small charts pay? | W-first at 3×120, W-page and W-load must not regress beyond noise. In practice this means the module is loaded lazily and only above the crossover size. |
   172	| Does the API survive? | `line()` stays synchronous and works before the module has loaded. WebAssembly instantiation is asynchronous, so the TypeScript path must remain as the default and the fallback. |
   173	| Does it run everywhere Axylo runs? | Script-tag build, Vite, webpack, Next.js, and a page whose Content Security Policy lacks `wasm-unsafe-eval` (the TypeScript path must take over without an error). No reliance on threads, which need cross-origin isolation that embedded dashboards rarely have. |
   174	| Are both paths the same chart? | Differential tests feed identical inputs to both implementations and require identical output for integer results and agreement within a stated tolerance for floating point, including F2 and F5 property tests on the Rust path. |
   175	| What does it cost to keep? | Recorded honestly: added toolchain (Rust, `wasm-bindgen` or equivalent) in every contributor's and CI's setup, native Windows build verified on Windows and not by cross-compiling, added bytes (lazy), CI minutes, lines of Rust, and the permanent obligation to maintain two implementations of one stage. |
   176	
   177	### 7.4 Decision
   178	
   179	Adopt only if every row passes and the end-to-end gain is at least 20% at a size users reach. The adoption record names the workload, the crossover size and the conditions under which the decision is reversed:
   180	
   181	- tuned TypeScript comes within 10% on a later browser release, checked at each quarterly comparison;
   182	- the differential tests cannot be kept green without disproportionate effort;
   183	- the fallback path is observed to be the one most users run.
   184	
   185	If the experiment misses, the record is kept as a negative result with its numbers, the tuned TypeScript stays, and the idea is not reopened without a new profile that changes precondition 1.
   186	
   187	An outcome where Rust wins the isolated stage by a large factor and the workload by a few percent is the expected failure mode. It means the stage was not the bottleneck, and the right response is to go back to step 2 of the loop.

1	# Phase 1b: Axylo product specification
     2	
     3	Based on the findings in [01-landscape.md](01-landscape.md). Finding IDs (R1–R16 for readers, D1–D10 for developers) refer to that document. Criterion IDs defined here are F, L, I, A (reader), DX (developer) and P (performance).
     4	
     5	## 1. What Axylo is
     6	
     7	**Axylo is the everyday chart you can ship without checking it.** The smallest correct call produces a chart that represents the data faithfully, stays readable at any width and in any color scheme, works with a keyboard and a screen reader, and stays fast at a million points. When the data is wrong, Axylo says so instead of drawing a guess.
     8	
     9	It is a framework-neutral TypeScript library under the MIT license, with a thin React adapter.
    10	
    11	### 1.1 Why someone would choose it
    12	
    13	Phase 1 found no library that holds these together. Each row is a reason to choose Axylo over the library a team would otherwise reach for.
    14	
    15	| If you would otherwise use | You get today | Axylo adds |
    16	|---|---|---|
    17	| Chart.js | Simple API, permissive license, widest reach | Keyboard and screen-reader access without author work, reduced-motion support, dates that do not shift, a tooltip that appears wherever the pointer is, large data without expert options, about half the bytes |
    18	| Recharts | The React default | A palette, a title, labels that fit, formatted numbers and dates without code, 100,000 points without seconds of blocking, the same chart outside React |
    19	| Highcharts | The best reader experience of the ten | The same class of accessibility with no module to import, no commercial license, a third of the bytes, reduced-motion support, useful errors |
    20	| ECharts or ApexCharts | Many chart types | Fewer types, each of which fits its labels, reports bad data and is accessible by default; a fraction of the bytes |
    21	| uPlot | The speed reference | Speed of the same order with automatic sizing, a palette, bars and donuts without path builders, and an accessibility layer |
    22	
    23	What Axylo does not try to win: number of chart types, visual customization depth, or exploratory analysis.
    24	
    25	### 1.2 Who it is for
    26	
    27	A developer adding charts to a product or an internal dashboard: data arrives as rows from an API, the chart is one component among many on the page, and the person writing it is not a visualization specialist and will not test it with a screen reader. Coding agents writing that code are the same audience: they benefit from one data shape, typed fields and diagnostics that say what to change.
    28	
    29	Not the audience for 1.0: analysts exploring data in notebooks, designers building bespoke graphics, and teams that need maps, financial charts or network diagrams.
    30	
    31	### 1.3 Principles
    32	
    33	| Principle | In practice |
    34	|---|---|
    35	| Correct before configurable | A default that can mislead (truncated bars, shifted dates, interpolated gaps) is a bug, even if an option fixes it. |
    36	| Say it, do not guess | Anything Axylo cannot draw faithfully becomes a diagnostic with a code, a location and a fix. |
    37	| Everything a reader needs is on; nothing else is | Title, units, legend, tooltip, keyboard, description and table are on. Entry animation, markers on dense lines and toolbars are not. |
    38	| One way to do each thing | One data shape, one update method, one place for colors (CSS). |
    39	| The page is the theme | Font, text color and color scheme come from the page; nothing is hardcoded that the page already decides. |
    40	
    41	## 2. Scope of the first release
    42	
    43	### 2.1 Chart types
    44	
    45	| Type | Variants | Typical question |
    46	|---|---|---|
    47	| Line | Multi-series, gaps, time or numeric x | How did it change over time? |
    48	| Area | Single, stacked | How did the total and its parts change? |
    49	| Bar | Vertical, horizontal, grouped, stacked | How do categories compare? |
    50	| Scatter | Optional series | How are two measures related? |
    51	| Donut | Up to eight slices | What share does each part have? |
    52	
    53	Plus, on every cartesian chart: reference lines and bands (a target, an incident window).
    54	
    55	The Phase 1 harness exercised line, bar and donut in all ten libraries (donut in nine; uPlot has none). Area and scatter are added on judgment. Phase 1 found no usage data by chart type, so the choice of five is a judgment about everyday dashboards, not a measured ranking.
    56	
    57	### 2.2 Workflows
    58	
    59	| # | Workflow | What it requires of Axylo |
    60	|---|---|---|
    61	| W1 | Show a query result | Rows in, chart out; field types inferred; bad rows reported. |
    62	| W2 | Fill a dashboard | Dozens of charts per page; container-sized; themed by the page; loading, empty and error states. |
    63	| W3 | Compare categories | Labels of any length; horizontal bars; grouped and stacked. |
    64	| W4 | Watch a live metric | Append without redraw cost growing; no animation jitter. |
    65	| W5 | Explore a time range | Tooltip anywhere, legend toggle, zoom and pan by pointer, touch and keyboard. |
    66	| W6 | Read it another way | Keyboard, screen reader, table view, high contrast, reduced motion, 400% zoom, color-vision deficiency. |
    67	
    68	## 3. Acceptance criteria: the reader's experience
    69	
    70	Every criterion has a test. "Probe" means the Phase 1 harness in `research/harness`, rerun with Axylo added. "Property test" means the statement is checked over at least 1,000 generated datasets.
    71	
    72	### 3.1 Faithful representation
    73	
    74	| ID | Criterion | Verified by | Driven by |
    75	|---|---|---|---|
    76	| F1 | Bar and area value axes include zero. A domain that excludes zero is only possible with `zero: false`, which draws an axis-break mark and adds the fact to the description. | Property test on domains; `bars` fixture (values 82–97) starts at 0 | R1 |
    77	| F2 | A missing value (`null`, `undefined`) is drawn as a gap: never as zero, never bridged. A value isolated between two gaps is drawn as a visible point. Tooltip, table and announcements say "No data". | `trend` and `dirty` fixtures; property test that no segment connects across a missing index | R5 |
    78	| F3 | Input that cannot be plotted faithfully is reported and not guessed. `NaN` and infinities: warning AX103, treated as missing. Numeric strings: warning AX104, not plotted unless `coerce: true`. Unparseable dates, duplicate x within a series, negative donut values, more series than palette entries: each has a code. `strict: true` throws. | `dirty` fixture yields exactly AX103 ×1 (row 3) and AX104 ×1 (row 4); Mon–Tue drawn as a segment, Sun as a point, Wed–Sat as gaps | R5, D5 |
    79	| F4 | A date without a time (`2026-02-24`) is a calendar date and reads the same in every viewer time zone. An instant is shown in the declared `timeZone` (default: the viewer's), and the zone is stated in the description. A date-time string without an offset is shown as written and raises a hint asking for `timeZone`. | `trend` rendered under UTC, America/Los_Angeles and Asia/Kolkata: identical tick labels and tooltip text | R3 |
    80	| F5 | No smoothing by default. When points outnumber pixels, the line shows the minimum and maximum of every pixel column. | One outlier in 1,000,000 points is visible at every zoom level; pixel comparison against an undecimated render stays within tolerance | D8, D9 |
    81	| F6 | Numbers and dates are formatted for the page locale. Axis ticks may be compact (`50K`); tooltip, table and announcements show the value at the data's own precision. No raw `Date` strings or epoch numbers appear anywhere. | `trend` fixture: axis shows grouped thousands; tooltip for 36,207 reads `36,207`; text scan finds no `GMT` or 13-digit number | R4 |
    82	| F7 | The axis domain contains all data and ends at the first tick at or above the maximum. A field whose label or format marks it as a percentage, with data at or below 100, ends at 100. | Property test; `bars` fixture ends at 100, not 125 | R1 |
    83	| F8 | Donut slices keep the given order, start at 12 o'clock and run clockwise. Each slice's value and percentage are readable as text without hovering. Negative values produce AX120 and no chart. More than eight slices produce a hint. The legend order equals the slice order. | `parts` fixture; diagnostics tests | R7, scoreboard 3.1 |
    84	| F9 | No two series share a color. Beyond eight series the chart raises AX130 and distinguishes the rest by dash or marker in addition to cycling. | Test with 6, 8 and 12 series | R7 |
    85	| F10 | Stacks place positive and negative values on their own sides of zero. A missing value inside a stack is reported, because a gap there changes the totals above it. | Property test on stacked geometry | R5 |
    86	
    87	### 3.2 Legibility
    88

   107	## 2. Method
   108	
   109	One Vite project loads each library from npm and runs the same tasks into a 720×400 container. A Playwright script drives system Chrome 157 (headless) through every combination and records screenshots, the DOM, the accessibility tree, keyboard and pointer behavior, and timings.
   110	
   111	**Rule for "default settings":** each task states what the reader must be able to do (see the data with axes and a title, tell series apart, read exact values). Each library gets the least configuration that its documentation needs for that, and no styling. Where a library cannot render at all without a choice (a color, a size), the value from its own documentation is used and the requirement is recorded.
   112	
   113	| Task | Data | What it tests |
   114	|---|---|---|
   115	| `trend` | 3 series × 120 daily values (UTC midnights), thousands to tens of thousands; one series has 7 missing days | Time axis, legend, tooltip, number formatting, gaps |
   116	| `bars` | 7 categories, values 82–97, one long category name | Zero baseline, label fitting |
   117	| `parts` | 6 shares, two under 3% | Part-to-whole labels, palette |
   118	| `dirty` | `[10, 20, null, NaN, '40', undefined, 70]` | What happens to bad input, and who is told |
   119	| `empty` | The `trend` chart with zero rows | Empty state |
   120	| `scale` | One series of 10,000, 100,000 and 1,000,000 points | Time to draw, default and documented fast path |
   121	| `stream` | 600-point window, one new point per frame for 300 frames | Update cost |
   122	
   123	Cross-cutting probes on `trend`: Tab and arrow-key walk; pointer hover with the browser in UTC and in America/Los_Angeles; container shrunk to 360 px; page rendered at 340 px; `prefers-color-scheme: dark`; first frame against settled frame with and without `prefers-reduced-motion`.
   124	
   125	What this method does not cover: Firefox and Safari; real screen readers (the accessibility tree was inspected, no reader was run); touch; right-to-left text; anything beyond each library's first-page configuration. Each library has options that fix most of what follows. The point of the study is what a reader gets when the author does the minimum, because that is what most everyday charts are.

     7	## 1. Public API
     8	
     9	### 1.1 Shape
    10	
    11	One function per chart type, each taking a target element and a plain options object, each returning the same small handle.
    12	
    13	```ts
    14	import { line } from 'axylo';
    15	
    16	const chart = line('#sessions', {
    17	  title: 'Daily sessions by channel',
    18	  data: rows,              // [{ day: '2026-01-01', channel: 'Direct', sessions: 31713 }, …]
    19	  x: 'day',
    20	  y: 'sessions',
    21	  series: 'channel',
    22	});
    23	```
    24	
    25	That is the whole first chart. Everything the reader needs (axes, legend, tooltip, keyboard access, description, data table, light and dark colors, resizing) is on without further options.
    26	
    27	Why this shape:
    28	
    29	| Decision | Reason |
    30	|---|---|
    31	| Rows of objects plus field names | Finding D2: the ten libraries take five incompatible data shapes, and every harness implementation started by reshaping the same rows. App data arrives as rows (JSON, SQL). |
    32	| One function per chart type (`line`, `area`, `bar`, `scatter`, `donut`) | Each has its own options type, so invalid combinations are type errors (DX3), and bundlers drop unused chart types (DX7). |
    33	| Plain options object, not a builder or JSX tree | It serializes, diffs, and is the same object in the React adapter. Recharts needed 8 JSX components for the trend task; the information content was four fields. |
    34	| No required configuration beyond data and fields | Findings R15, R11, D1: tooltips, legends, time adapters, margins, colors and accessibility were opt-in somewhere in every library. |
    35	
    36	### 1.2 Fields
    37	
    38	A field is a key of the row type, or an object when it needs more.
    39	
    40	```ts
    41	line(el, {
    42	  data: rows,
    43	  x: { field: 'ts', timeZone: 'UTC' },
    44	  y: { field: 'sessions', label: 'Sessions', format: { notation: 'compact' } },
    45	  series: 'channel',
    46	});
    47	
    48	// wide rows: one column per series
    49	line(el, { data: wide, x: 'day', y: ['direct', 'organic', 'referral'] });
    50	```
    51	
    52	| Option | Meaning |
    53	|---|---|
    54	| `field` | Key of the row. Typed as `keyof Row`, so a typo fails to compile. |
    55	| `label` | Axis title and the name used in tooltip, table and announcements. Defaults to the field name; a diagnostic suggests setting it when the field name looks like an identifier. |

1	# Phase 1a: the browser charting landscape, November 2026
     2	
     3	Evidence collected 2026-11-17. Scripts, raw data and screenshots are in [`research/`](../research/README.md).
     4	
     5	## Summary
     6	
     7	Ten widely used libraries were given the same five reader-facing tasks and two load tasks, with the least configuration each one needs. No library passed all of them, and the failures cluster in three places that Axylo can own:
     8	
     9	1. **Charts that are wrong or unreadable without anyone being told.** None of the ten reported a string, a `NaN` or an `undefined` in the data. Four plotted the string as a number, four lost the series or the whole chart, one drew a line across the missing days, and the hand-built D3 chart lost everything after the second point. Six showed a daily value on the previous day to a reader in Los Angeles. Two silently removed the category label that did not fit, and a third removed five of seven.
    10	2. **Accessibility that depends on the author doing extra work.** Five of ten exposed nothing usable to a keyboard or a screen reader. Four animate regardless of the reader's reduced-motion setting. Two were legible on a dark page without configuration. No default palette both reached 3:1 contrast and stayed distinguishable under simulated color-vision deficiency.
    11	3. **A gap between "easy" and "fast".** Six of ten took between 1.9 seconds and more than 45 seconds to draw a million points with default options; the one that drew them in about 60 ms needed hand-set sizes, colors and time units and has no accessibility layer.
    12	
    13	The strongest single library on the reader's side was Highcharts (with its accessibility module imported): it alone wrapped the long label, adapted to dark mode by design, and generated a description of the chart. It is commercially licensed, 143 kB gzipped for three chart types, ignores reduced motion, and threw an unhelpful error on dirty input.

     5	## 1. What Axylo is
     6	
     7	**Axylo is the everyday chart you can ship without checking it.** The smallest correct call produces a chart that represents the data faithfully, stays readable at any width and in any color scheme, works with a keyboard and a screen reader, and stays fast at a million points.      8	
     9	It is a framework-neutral TypeScript library under the MIT license, with a thin React adapter.
    10	
    11	### 1.1 Why someone would choose it
    12	
    13	Phase 1 found no library that holds these together. Each row is a reason to choose Axylo over the library a team would otherwise reach for.
    14

    16	|---|---|---|

    18	| Recharts | The React default | A palette, a title, labels that fit, formatted numbers and dates without code, 100,000 points without seconds of blocking, the same chart outside React |
    19	| Highcharts | The best reader experience of the ten | The same class of accessibility with no module to import, no commercial license, a third of the bytes, reduced-motion support, useful errors |

    21	| uPlot | The speed reference | Speed of the same order with automatic sizing, a palette, bars and donuts without path builders, and an accessibility layer |
    22

    24

110	## 5. What makes a gain worth shipping
   111	
   112	All of the following must hold.
   113	
   114	| Condition | Threshold |
   115	|---|---|
   116	| The gain is real | The 95% confidence interval for the improvement in the target metric excludes zero, and the median improvement is at least twice that session's noise floor. |
   117	| The gain is large enough to matter | At least 5% on the target workload's primary metric, or it moves a workload from failing to passing its budget, or it removes at least one frame over budget per 300 in a pacing workload. |
   118	| Nothing else pays for it | No other tracked workload regresses by more than its noise floor or 2%, whichever is larger. This is checked in all three browsers. |
   119	| Bytes are accounted for | At most 0.3 kB gzipped per 5% gained on the target workload, and the DX7 size budget still holds. Larger costs need a workload moving from fail to pass. |
   120	| Correctness is unchanged | Scene snapshots are identical, or every difference is reviewed and approved. All fidelity property tests pass, in particular F2 (gaps) and F5 (extremes survive decimation). |
   121	| Complexity is paid for | A change that adds a new code path, a mode or a public option needs at least 20% on its target, or a budget moving from fail to pass. Otherwise the simpler code stays. |
   122	
   123	A gain a reader cannot perceive (for example 9 ms to 7 ms on a one-off render) ships only if it is free in bytes and complexity. Crossing a threshold a reader can perceive ranks above any percentage: one frame (16.7 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz) for interaction and animation, 100 ms for a response to input, 1 s for a chart to appear.
   124	
   125	## 6. Catching regressions
   126	
   127	| When | What runs | Compared with | Action |
   128	|---|---|---|---|
   129	| Every pull request | Smoke set: W-first at 3×120 and 1×100k, W-stream at 600, W-hover at 100k, bytes. Chromium, 10 interleaved runs, about 3 minutes. | The merge base, built and run in the same job | Fail on a regression over 10% with a confidence interval excluding zero, or any size-budget breach. Otherwise post the table. |
   130	| Nightly | Full workload set, three browsers, desktop and throttled profiles, 20 runs | The previous night and the last release | Open an issue for any workload outside its noise band two nights running, with the commit range. |
   131	| Before a release | Full set plus the phone profile, Edge on Windows, and the comparison libraries | Budgets P1–P7 and the previous release | A failed budget blocks the release, or the budget is changed in the spec with a written reason. Never silently. |
   132	| Quarterly | Comparison library versions bumped; budgets expressed as ratios re-derived | – | Publish the updated comparison. |
   133	
   134	Pull-request runs use shared CI machines, so they compare two builds inside one job and never against stored numbers. Nightly and release runs use the reference machine and are the only source of absolute numbers.
   135	
   136	Results are appended to `bench/history/` as one JSON file per run with commit, browser versions, machine profile, noise floor and raw samples. A page in the documentation site charts that history with Axylo itself.
   137	
   138	Performance tests are held to the same honesty rules as functional tests: a budget is not relaxed to make a run pass, a known-slow workload is reported as failing until it is fixed, and a comparison that Axylo loses is published as measured.
   139	
   140	## 7. Where Rust could be justified, and what it would take
   141	
   142	### 7.1 Candidates
   143	
   144	A Rust experiment is worth running only for a stage that is a measured bottleneck on a tracked workload and is compute-bound on numeric data. Stages that mostly call browser APIs cannot gain: each call crosses the JavaScript–WebAssembly boundary and the browser does the work either way.
   145	
   146	| Stage | Could Rust help? | Reasoning |
   147	|---|---|---|
   148	| Decimation and aggregation over typed columns (min–max per pixel, binning, stacking) at 1M+ points | Possibly | Tight numeric loops over contiguous memory; SIMD is available in WebAssembly. JavaScript engines already compile such loops well, so the expected gain is small multiples at best. |
   149	| Spatial index build and query for scatter at 1M+ points | Possibly | Memory layout control matters; no browser API involved. |
   150	| Parsing large text inputs (CSV, ISO dates) into columns | Unlikely | Strings must be copied into WebAssembly memory and decoded; the copy often costs as much as the parse. |
   151	| Layout, tick generation, label fitting | No | Small inputs; dominated by text measurement, which is a browser call. |
   152	| Canvas 2D drawing | No | One boundary crossing per command. |
   153	| Rendering to a pixel buffer or to WebGL/WebGPU from Rust | Only as a separate product decision | It replaces the renderer rather than accelerating a stage, brings its own text rendering, and does nothing for the DOM-based accessibility layer. It would need a failing raster-bound budget that item 9 in section 4 could not fix in TypeScript. |
   154	
   155	### 7.2 Preconditions for starting an experiment
   156	
   157	1. A profile shows the stage holds at least 30% of blocking time on a tracked workload at a size users reach, and that workload fails its budget or is the largest remaining wait.
   158	2. The TypeScript version of that stage has already been tuned (typed arrays, no allocation in the loop, monomorphic call sites, pixel-bounded work) and independently reviewed as tuned. "Tuned" is a recorded claim with a profile attached, not an impression.
   159	3. The experiment has a written hypothesis with a number and a time ceiling.
   160	
   161	### 7.3 Evidence required to adopt
   162	
   163	The comparison is always end to end, on the workload, against the tuned TypeScript build, with section 3's method.
   164	
   165	| Question | Evidence required |
   166	|---|---|
   167	| Is the workload faster for the reader? | Median improvement of at least 20% on the workload's primary metric (not on the isolated function), confidence interval excluding zero, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari. A function-level microbenchmark is not evidence. |
   168	| What does startup cost? | Fetch, compile and instantiate time of the `.wasm`, cold and warm cache, on desktop and throttled profiles, included in W-load and in the first render of the affected workload. Stated as the number of operations needed to earn the startup cost back. |
   169	| What does data transfer cost? | Time to move columns into WebAssembly memory and results back, measured separately and included in the end-to-end number. If the design keeps columns in WebAssembly memory to avoid copies, the cost that imposes on `update`, `append` and memory (P7) is measured too. |
   170	| Where is the crossover? | The data size above which the Rust path wins end to end, including the costs above. It must be at or below sizes real users reach; a win only at 50M points is not a reason. |
   171	| Do small charts pay? | W-first at 3×120, W-page and W-load must not regress beyond noise. In practice this means the module is loaded lazily and only above the crossover size. |
   172	| Does the API survive? | `line()` stays synchronous and works before the module has loaded. WebAssembly instantiation is asynchronous, so the TypeScript path must remain as the default and the fallback. |
   173	| Does it run everywhere Axylo runs? | Script-tag build, Vite, webpack, Next.js, and a page whose Content Security Policy lacks `wasm-unsafe-eval` (the TypeScript path must take over without an error). No reliance on threads, which need cross-origin isolation that embedded dashboards rarely have. |
   174	| Are both paths the same chart? | Differential tests feed identical inputs to both implementations and require identical output for integer results and agreement within a stated tolerance for floating point, including F2 and F5 property tests on the Rust path. |
   175	| What does it cost to keep? | Recorded honestly: added toolchain (Rust, `wasm-bindgen` or equivalent) in every contributor's and CI's setup, native Windows build verified on Windows and not by cross-compiling, added bytes (lazy), CI minutes, lines of Rust, and the permanent obligation to maintain two implementations of one stage. |
   176	
   177	### 7.4 Decision
   178	
   179	Adopt only if every row passes and the end-to-end gain is at least 20% at a size users reach. The adoption record names the workload, the crossover size and the conditions under which the decision is reversed:
   180	
   181	- tuned TypeScript comes within 10% on a later browser release, checked at each quarterly comparison;
   182	- the differential tests cannot be kept green without disproportionate effort;
   183	- the fallback path is observed to be the one most users run.
   184	
   185	If the experiment misses, the record is kept as a negative result with its numbers, the tuned TypeScript stays, and the idea is not reopened without a new profile that changes precondition 1.
   186	
   187	An outcome where Rust wins the isolated stage by a large factor and the workload by a few percent is the expected failure mode. It means the stage was not the bottleneck, and the right response is to go back to step 2 of the loop.

## Findings

### B1. The rendered scene cannot supply the exact data promised to readers

- Where: [Product spec, F2, F5, I1 and A1–A4](/home/canarit/projects/axylo/docs/02-product-spec.md:74), [TypeScript plan, §2.1–2.2](/home/canarit/projects/axylo/docs/03-plan-typescript-release.md:143)
- Evidence: **Observed.** The scene tags each primitive with a datum reference. The accessibility layer and hit index consume that scene, and dense lines keep only selected values. A4 exposes the first 1,000 rows. **Inferred.** A path can represent many observations, including values that were never emitted as vertices. Scene tags alone cannot recover those observations, missing-value positions, or exact ordinals. A reader can also see a spike near row 900,000 and have no way to retrieve it through the table.
- Change: Make a versioned, lossless normalized frame the source for exact lookup, summaries, navigation and the table. Derive geometry and interaction coordinates from the same frame revision and visibility state. Build the table on demand with native pagination and a way to jump by x or category. Test a million-point chart where a decimated-away value, a late spike and an explicit gap are all retrievable. Specify whether each surface describes the visible range or the full dataset.

### B2. A fixed number of vertices per pixel cannot preserve every gap and isolated point

- Where: [Product spec, F2, F5 and L5](/home/canarit/projects/axylo/docs/02-product-spec.md:77), [TypeScript plan, §2.2 and M6](/home/canarit/projects/axylo/docs/03-plan-typescript-release.md:173)
- Evidence: **Observed.** F5 triggers when points outnumber pixels. The plan triggers above twice the plot width and keeps first, min, max and last per column. F2 and L5 require every isolated point and forbid bridging gaps. **Inferred.** A column can contain hundreds of alternating valid and missing samples. Four vertices can lose isolated values or join separate runs. An O(visible points) scan also remains a redraw cost at full zoom, even if canvas commands are bounded.
